summary: This continuation develops uniform definitions of geometric prime divisors of finitely generated fields and uses them to define finite normalizations, obtain parametric bi-interpretability with the integers and characterize each finitely generated field by one ring sentence within that class. The characteristic-two resolution hypothesis is imposed exactly above Kronecker dimension three. Functional transcendence is assigned to a separate continuation by the accompanying restructuring proposal.

nodes.title: The field hypothesis H_d
nodes.statement: For an integer d≥3, H_d(K) means Field.FG(K), δ(K)=d, and, only if char K=2 and d>3, resolution above F₂ in the two-clause sense HL.6/resolution-f2. Here δ(K)=trdeg(K/prime field)+1 in characteristic zero and trdeg(K/prime field) otherwise. The resolution clause is a genuine geometric proposition, not a dummy boolean or a local-field axiom.
hypotheses: d is a fixed integer, d≥3.
proofSteps: Use Field.FG and the imported dimension convention, retaining its prime-field shift.
Import both birational resolution and smooth SNC compactification from HL.6/resolution-f2.

nodes.title: Uniform definable families with empty fibers
nodes.statement: For a fixed natural m and a ring formula Φ(x;y₁,…,y_m), the fiber in a field K at b∈K^m is {x∈K:K satisfies Φ(x;b)}. A family of subrings or valuation rings is uniformly definable on a class C if one such m and Φ give every member on every K∈C and every fiber is either an allowed member or empty. Formula and arity are independent of K; repetitions of the same subset are allowed.
hypotheses: The object variable has one field coordinate; parameter length m is fixed for the class.
proofSteps: Use the existing ring language and its semantics.
Admissibility can be conjoined to a raw fiber formula; failed tuples then give the empty set.

sources.match: Uniformity includes both exhaustion of divisors and control of every parameter fiber.

acceptance: Reject a scheme with one new formula per valuation.

nodes.title: Fixed arithmetic dimension is first-order
nodes.statement: For each n≥0 there is a parameter-free ring sentence Dim_n whose models among finitely generated fields are exactly those of Kronecker dimension n. There is no assertion that the collection of finitely generated fields is elementary.
hypotheses: Only the equivalence on Field.FG structures is asserted.
proofSteps: Use Poonen Theorem 2.3 and its Pop proof contract: characteristic-dependent degree-two or degree-three diagonal-form isotropy bounds and separating specializations characterize finite transcendence degree.
Retain the characteristic-zero dimension shift; the published Pop numbering and proof remain the explicit G-DIM audit leaf.

sources.match: This is exactly the fixed-dimension sentence used to filter definable subfields.

acceptance: Dim₀ holds on finite fields and fails on Q.
Do not replace finite arithmetic dimension by finite cardinality.

nodes.title: Global arithmetic formula inputs
nodes.statement: In the class of global fields, one fixed-arity formula family exhausts the nontrivial finite valuation rings, with every fiber either such a ring or empty. Number fields are first-order distinguishable from global function fields. The integer ring of a number field and the finite constant field of a global function field are uniformly definable; with a suitable transcendental parameter in a global function field, the polynomial subring and the powers needed for arithmetic sequence coding are definable.
hypotheses: The function-field polynomial subring is the distinguished rational polynomial ring in the chosen parameter, not automatically the full ring of functions regular outside an arbitrary point.
proofSteps: Take the precise uniformity clauses from Rumely Introduction I–III as cited in Poonen Theorem 2.2.

First establish these formulas in an ambient global field. Later consumers use LD.0 to relativize them to an already definable global subfield; the present theorem does not depend on constructing that subfield family.
Keep G-RUM open until the original proofs of the valuation family, integer ring and coding apparatus have been audited; their statements are not a new axiom of fields.

sources.match: The quoted theorem contracts from Rumely distinguish the global-field types and uniformly define their arithmetic subrings and finite valuation rings.
The dimension-one arithmetic coding argument identifies the polynomial and sequence-decoding inputs supplied by Rumely.
The global arithmetic families are consumed by the low-dimensional divisor construction and the arithmetic normalization argument.

acceptance: The valuation family for a number field includes all finite primes, not its real orderings.
The polynomial-ring assertion must retain its distinguished transcendental parameter.

nodes.title: Characteristic-zero constants from elliptic probes
nodes.statement: There is one ring formula C₀(x) defining the relative algebraic closure κ of Q in every finitely generated characteristic-zero field K and defining the empty set in positive characteristic.
hypotheses: K is finitely generated as a field.
proofSteps: Use Moret–Bailly’s elliptic curve with E(Q) infinite and E(K)=E(κ) to produce a definable set S⊆κ whose rational points are dense at each finite rational place.

The quotient of two nonzero x/y elliptic parameters supplies local density. After adjoining a root of −1, quantify isotropy of three-fold Pfister forms with slots s₁,s₂,t−s₃. Constants pass by the nonreal number-field bound; a nonconstant t fails at a smooth specialization and a split place.
Keep only candidate sets which are fields of arithmetic dimension one and number-field type; their union is κ. Use G-PO for the external elliptic existence and coding proof audits.

sources.match: The elliptic probes and field filters give the constants without an unbounded algebraic-degree predicate.

acceptance: For K=Q(t), the output is Q, not Q(t).
The same formula has empty output on F₅(t).

nodes.title: Global function subfields from elliptic twists
nodes.statement: There is a fixed-arity ring-definable family whose members, in every finitely generated positive-characteristic K, are exactly its relatively algebraically closed global function subfields. For finite K that family is empty.
hypotheses: No restriction on characteristic two; formulas use general nonsingular Weierstrass equations.
proofSteps: Use an ordinary elliptic curve over the finite constants. Nearly-prime point counts and the Weil bound make the two z-coordinate sums meet an arbitrary smooth image in A¹×E (Poonen Lemmas 4.1–4.6).
Choose a ramified quadratic twist not isogenous to any simple factor of the Albanese of a model of K/L. Every map to this twist is constant, giving E_u(K)=E_u(L).
The degree-d diagonal form with d=3 in characteristic two and d=2 otherwise detects nonmembers by two regular parameters; local anisotropy survives purely inseparable extensions of degree prime to d.

Adjoin a root of X²+X+1, use the family there and intersect with K; retain field fibers of dimension one. The finite étale split case must be encoded as a field factor, not an integral quotient assumed without proof. External elliptic/Albanese inputs are G-PO.

sources.match: The construction uniformly exhausts the relatively closed one-dimensional function subfields, including characteristic two.

acceptance: For F₂(s,t), every relative closure of F₂(as+bt) with a,b not both zero must occur.
No quadratic-only substitution for the cubic diagonal forms is valid in characteristic two.

nodes.title: Uniform definition of the constant field
nodes.statement: One parameter-free ring formula C(x) defines κ, the relative algebraic closure of the prime field, in every finitely generated field K, including finite K.
hypotheses: The constant field is finite in positive characteristic and a number field in characteristic zero.
proofSteps: Use char-zero-constants in characteristic zero, separated from positive characteristic by Poonen’s characteristic sentence.

In positive characteristic intersect the uniformly definable constant fields of all relatively closed global function subfields. If K is finite, this is the empty-family intersection K, correctly equal to κ.
Use the Rumely global constant-field formula inside each interpreted subfield; its proof-audit contract is G-RUM.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.3,p.2 and its proof,p.11; Theorem 1.1,p.1; Theorem 2.2,pp.3–4
sources.match: The empty global-subfield family gives the correct finite-field boundary.

acceptance: For K=F₉, C defines all of K; for F₉(t), exactly F₉.

nodes.title: Uniform maximal global subfields
nodes.statement: On every infinite finitely generated field K, the relatively algebraically closed global subfields form a uniform definable family. In characteristic zero its unique member is κ; in positive characteristic it is the preceding family.
hypotheses: A global field means arithmetic dimension one, not an algebraically closed field.
proofSteps: Combine the characteristic-zero constant-field definition with positive-global-subfields.
Use the explicit field/dimension filters; arbitrary fibers which fail the filters are empty.

sources.match: The construction consumes a uniformly definable relatively closed global subfield.
The positive-characteristic family and the characteristic-zero constant field provide the two branches.

acceptance: For Q(s,t), κ is a number field and is the only allowed global base.
A merely global but not relatively closed subfield does not pass this family’s contract.

nodes.title: Uniform relative and absolute algebraic independence
nodes.statement: For each fixed n, algebraic dependence of n elements over a named relatively closed global subfield L is expressed by a ring formula with its subfield predicate. Algebraic dependence over the prime field is also uniformly expressible in every finitely generated field. Negating these formulas defines independence.
hypotheses: For the relative assertion K/L is finitely generated and L is relatively algebraically closed in K.
proofSteps: For n=0 the empty tuple is independent over every field; choose the always-false dependence formula. Use the following construction only for n≥1.
After adjoining roots of −1 and X²+X+1, use diagonal forms with degree d=3 in characteristic two and d=2 otherwise. Dependent tuples pass the C-field/global bound.

For an independent tuple pass to the maximal separable subextension over a transcendence basis, choose an étale specialization, then a global place split in its residue extension. A non-d-th-power residue and a uniformizer give the anisotropic initial form. Append the regular parameters using the distinct-values-mod-d argument of Appendix A.4–A.5.

Purely inseparable descent uses odd-degree quadratic descent or degree-three descent across quadratic extensions. These degree-three inputs are part of G-PO, not a consequence of quadratic Pfister theory.

For absolute dependence in positive characteristic, either the first element is constant, or choose a relatively closed global L containing it and test the other n−1 elements relatively. In characteristic zero test over κ.

sources.locator: Lemma 5.3 and proof of Theorem 1.4,pp.11–12; Appendix A,pp.13–14
sources.match: Relative dependence is proved with degree-sensitive local forms; the global subfield family then gives absolute dependence.

acceptance: Over Q, (s,s²) is dependent and (s,t) independent in Q(s,t).
Over F₂(s), t is transcendental in F₂(s,t); the cubic branch must return independence.
At n=0 the dependence formula is false, including over finite fields; its negation defines the independence of the empty tuple.

nodes.title: The relative constant field k_t
nodes.statement: Let k₁⊂K be a relatively closed global subfield and u=(u₂,…,u_{d−1}) be algebraically independent over it. Set t_i=u_i²−u_i and k_t to be the relative algebraic closure of k₁(t) in K. Then k_t=k_u and K/k_t is a one-variable function field; k_t membership is uniformly definable at fixed d.
hypotheses: H_d(K); d−2 elements u_i.
proofSteps: The extension k₁(u)/k₁(t) is finite separable: each coordinate satisfies X²−X−t_i with nonzero derivative at u_i.
Relative algebraic closure is unchanged across an algebraic base extension.
An element x belongs to k_t precisely when (u₂,…,u_{d−1},x) is algebraically dependent over k₁.

sources.match: The relative constant field turns geometric divisors into one-variable places.

acceptance: Do not replace k_t by k₁ or by the ring k₁[t].

uses.how: restricts θ to the nonzero relative constants
requires the final detecting divisor to be trivial on this field

nodes.title: Nice Pfister presentations
nodes.statement: For H_d(K), a global subfield k₁ and nonzero slots a_d,…,a₀∈K, the presentation is k₁-nice if a₁,a₀∈k₁ and its two-fold tail q_{a₁,a₀} is isotropic over each real closure of k₁ and over k₁,v at every finite place v which is dyadic, has v(a₀)≠0 or has v(a₁)<0. Here k₁,v is the henselization at a finite place. In characteristic two the outer factors are bilinear and the quadratic last factor is x²+xy+a₀y².
hypotheses: All slots are nonzero; niceness refers to a presentation, not merely its isometry class.
proofSteps: Use the imported all-characteristic quadratic Pfister construction.
Package the three finite-place triggers and the real-place condition as a predicate on the slots and subfield.
First-order expressibility is a separate theorem in FG.4.

sources.match: Niceness excludes real and dyadic obstructions while allowing an anisotropic tail at selected good places.

acceptance: A condition checking only dyadic places is weaker and unusable.

uses.how: forces detecting prime divisors away from bad places
rules out a nontrivial restriction of the coarsened valuation to k₁

api.name: NicePresentation.real_isotropic

nodes.title: Approximation for the selected nice tail
nodes.statement: Let l₁/k₁ be finite separable global fields and Σ a finite set of finite places. After adding dyadic places, choose distinct v₁,v₀ outside Σ, with v₁ split in l₁ and a₀ a unit at every place of Σ and at v₁ defining a nonsplit quadratic residue extension there, while v₀ splits in k₁(α₀). Then one can choose a₁ with v₁(a₁)=1, v(a₁)=0 for v∈Σ, a₁ a local norm at all real/dyadic places and all v with v(a₀)≠0, and v(a₁)≥0 at every finite v≠v₀.
hypotheses: α₀ is a root of X²−a₀ in odd characteristic and X²−X−a₀ in characteristic two.
All requested local norm conditions are open neighborhoods of 1, and the exceptional pole v₀ splits in the quadratic extension.
proofSteps: Choose the split places using number-field or degree-sensitive function-field Chebotarev, avoiding a finite forbidden set.
Choose a₀ by weak approximation; irreducibility of the residue polynomial is open.

Apply strong approximation off the single finite place v₀, retaining the archimedean norm neighborhoods in number fields. This precise extension is requested from GlobalNumberFields Layer 6, not inferred from finite-adèle density alone.
For global function fields use the existing function-field strong approximation with constants finite; all other finite places are required integral.

sources.match: Only this simultaneous norm, valuation and single-exception integrality contract is used to construct nice tails.

acceptance: An approximation allowing uncontrolled poles away from v₀ does not prove niceness.

nodes.title: Nice tails surviving a separable extension
nodes.statement: For every finite separable extension l₁/k₁ of global fields and finite Σ⊂P_fin(k₁), there are a₁,a₀∈k₁×, units at Σ, such that q_{a₁,a₀} is k₁-nice and remains anisotropic over l₁.
hypotheses: No claim is made for arbitrary inseparable l₁/k₁ in this construction.
proofSteps: Use global-approximation-input. At the split place v₁ the nonsplit quadratic residue norm and odd value v₁(a₁)=1 give anisotropy; l₁ embeds in the completion at that split place.
At each real/dyadic or a₀-bad place the local norm condition gives isotropy. The only possible negative value of a₁ is at v₀, where the quadratic extension splits, also giving isotropy.

sources.match: The two distinct split places separate the anisotropic witness from the harmless exceptional pole.

acceptance: The tail remains anisotropic after the specified l₁ extension.
Its slots are units at every place of the originally prescribed Σ.

nodes.title: Parameters adapted to a geometric divisor
nodes.statement: For every geometric prime divisor w of H_d(K), there are a relatively closed global k₁⊂K and d−2 elements u_i algebraically independent over k₁ such that w is trivial on k₁(u), Kw/k₁(u) is finite separable, and adjoining any u_d with w(u_d)=1 gives a separating transcendence basis of K/k₁.
hypotheses: Residue embeddings are part of the assertion; K and Kw have the same characteristic.
proofSteps: In characteristic zero lift a residue transcendence basis; in positive characteristic lift a separating basis, use one lifted coordinate to form k₁ by relative algebraic closure and keep the other d−2 coordinates.
For a chosen uniformizer u_d, independence follows because the valuation is trivial on k₁(u) but nontrivial on u_d.

In the maximal separable intermediate field, the remaining purely inseparable extension has a unique valuation prolongation, ramification index one and residue degree one. The full one-variable fundamental equality, including inseparable extensions, forces its degree to be one.

sources.match: Residue separability and the inseparable fundamental equality are both required; a separable-only curve theorem is insufficient.

acceptance: The number of residue parameters is d−2 in both characteristics.
A residue transcendence basis without the separability condition is insufficient.

nodes.title: Test presentations over a global base
nodes.statement: For H_d(K), global k₁⊂K, a k₁-independent tuple t=(t₂,…,t_{d−1}) and a_d∈K×, a k₁,t-test presentation consists of a nice tail (a₁,a₀) and ε_i∈k₁× with a_i=t_i−ε_i for 2≤i<d, such that ε_i is a v-unit at every finite place v of k₁ with v(a₁)>0. Its form is q_{a_d,…,a₀}.
hypotheses: Every slot is nonzero; independence implies t_i−ε_i≠0.
proofSteps: Attach the shifts and their global unit conditions to a nice presentation.
Retain the unit condition under the encoding of parameters; its logical definability is proved in FG.4.

sources.match: The shifts impose the coefficient nonnegativity used before taking a compact limit.

acceptance: Do not quantify only over places where v(a₁)<0.

uses.how: constructs these presentations at a given divisor
makes ε_i units when the global restriction is nontrivial

api.statement: For each 2≤i<d, a_i=t_i−ε_i with ε_i∈k₁×.

nodes.title: Specialization into iterated Laurent fields
nodes.statement: Let l/k₁(t₂,…,t_{d−1}) be finite separable with k₁ global. On a nonempty open subset of the torus Spec k₁[t_i,t_i⁻¹], its normalization is finite étale. For a closed point above an allowed ε∈(k₁×)^{d−2}, the residue field k_ε/k₁ is finite separable, π_i=t_i−ε_i is a regular parameter system, and there are compatible field embeddings l→Frac(k_ε[[π₂,…,π_{d−1}]])→k_ε((π₂))⋯((π_{d−1})).
hypotheses: The completion identification uses the chosen coefficient-field lift over the étale neighborhood; it is not asserted for an arbitrary singular local ring.
proofSteps: Import finite generic normalization from A0-extension/arithmetic-normalization.
At an étale point, identify the completion with a formal power-series ring over its finite separable residue field. This general formal-étale completion comparison is requested from A0-extension.
Order the parameters and embed the multivariate fraction field into the iterated Laurent series field.

sources.match: The explicit embeddings let anisotropy over the residue extension propagate to the original residue field.

acceptance: All ε_i are nonzero because the chosen base is a torus.
Do not assume that a finite normalization is étale everywhere.

nodes.title: Abundance of anisotropic test forms
nodes.statement: Given a geometric prime divisor w of H_d(K), a global k₁ and independent t_i with w trivial on k₁(t) and Kw/k₁(t) finite separable, there is a dense open subset U of the (d−2)-dimensional k₁-torus such that each ε∈U(k₁) admits a nice tail (a₁,a₀) for which, for every a_d with odd w(a_d), q_{a_d,t−ε,a₁,a₀} is a k₁,t-test form and is anisotropic over K_w.
hypotheses: The quantifier over a_d follows the choice of the tail; the same tail works for every odd-valued a_d.
proofSteps: Use etale-specialization-input for l=Kw and an allowed ε, obtaining k_ε.

Let Σ contain every finite zero and pole of each ε_i, as well as the dyadic places. Apply global-nice-tail for l₁=k_ε. Since a₁ is a Σ-unit, every place with positive v(a₁) lies outside Σ and each ε_i is a unit there.
Append the independent Laurent-parameter values to the anisotropic tail using Q2.4/independent-values. Restrict back to Kw, then append the odd-valued a_d to lift anisotropy to K_w.

sources.match: The tail is chosen after specialization and the Σ choice proves the extra test-unit condition.

acceptance: The source’s subscript for the specialized form is interpreted as the residue form, not the original full K-form.
Negative odd values of a_d are allowed in this abundance theorem.

nodes.title: Prime-divisor detection of nice forms
nodes.statement: If H_d(K) holds and q_a is an anisotropic nice (d+1)-fold quadratic Pfister presentation over K, then some prime divisor w of K has q_a anisotropic over its henselization K_w.
hypotheses: The presentation includes a global k₁ and satisfies FG.1/nice-form.
proofSteps: Translate anisotropy to a nonzero class in H^{d+1}(K,Z/2(d)) using the imported invariant-zero and naturality theorems.
In characteristic two, apply HL.6/lgp-characteristic-two on a smooth projective model, retaining its unconditional d≤3 clause and its resolution premise above three.
In other characteristics apply HL.6/lgp-global-base after replacing k₁ by its relative algebraic closure when needed. The nonzero local tail and niceness force a finite non-dyadic constant place.

Use Gabber’s prime-to-two regular alteration over that henselian global valuation ring. Odd-degree restriction stays injective, and HL.6/lgp-good-model detects the class at a codimension-one point. Restrict that valuation to K; algebraic-extension residue dimension and henselization inclusions give the required prime divisor. The alteration source/proof is the precise G-ALT leaf.

sources.match: The three local–global inputs and the odd-degree alteration yield the detecting divisor; arbitrary-degree alterations do not.

acceptance: Do not use finite mod-two cohomological dimension for a global field with real places.
The characteristic-two resolution assumption is absent at d=3.

nodes.title: Parity and bad-place exclusion
nodes.statement: For an anisotropic nice presentation over H_d(K), every prime divisor w where q_a remains anisotropic is non-dyadic, has w(a₀)=0 and w(a₁)≥0, and has odd w(a_i) for at least one 1≤i≤d.
hypotheses: All prime divisors are normalized to integer value group.
proofSteps: Restrict w to the global k₁. A nontrivial restriction is a global place; niceness excludes all bad triggers.
If all a_i for i≥1 have even value, divide by squares of a uniformizer to make them units. Apply the imported finite-dimension unit-isotropy theorem; real-place isotropy follows from the nice tail.

sources.match: The parity statement is about some outer slot, not automatically a_d.

acceptance: The parity of a_d alone follows only after the other slots have become units.

nodes.title: Auxiliary root fields
nodes.statement: For a_d∈K×, θ∈K× and τ∈K, choose roots α,β in an algebraic closure of K satisfying α²−α=a_d/θ² and β²−β=τ²/a_d. Define K_θ=K(α), K_τ=K(β) and K_{θ,τ}=K(α,β). These are fields, finite separable of degrees at most two, two and four respectively, allowing degree one; their K-isomorphism types and the anisotropy of a K-form on them do not depend on root choices.
hypotheses: K is a field in any characteristic; a_d and θ are nonzero.
proofSteps: Use simple algebraic subfields of an algebraic closure, not the unreduced polynomial quotient.
In characteristic two the derivative is −1. In odd characteristic an irreducible quadratic is separable; a repeated root is already in K.
The alternative roots are 1−α and 1−β, which generate the same subfields. The composite has the stated tower bound.

acceptance: When τ=0, K_τ=K.

nodes.title: Nonnegative lower slots in root-field detectors
nodes.statement: In the setup of Proposition 3.10, fix N>0 and a detecting prime divisor w̃ of L(α_N) for q_a, where L/K is finite separable, t_i=u_i²−u_i and θ_N=(a_{d−1}⋯a₁)^N. Then w̃(a_i)≥0 for every i<d, and w̃(a₀)=0.
hypotheses: q_a is a k₁,t-test form for a_d and remains anisotropic over L(α_N).
proofSteps: If w̃ restricts nontrivially to k₁, the nice tail is anisotropic at that global henselization. The unit-isotropy criterion then forces positive value on a₁, so the test condition makes every ε_i a unit. If the restriction is trivial the same ε-unit conclusion is immediate.

If a_i=u_i²−u_i−ε_i has negative value, then u_i has negative value and a_i=u_i²(1−1/u_i−ε_i/u_i²). The parenthesized factor is a principal unit. Its two-fold Pfister tail is isotropic by Q2.4/principal-unit, a contradiction.

sources.match: The corrected negative sign in the ε term is necessary for the exact factorization.

acceptance: The argument uses an outer slot with the last quadratic factor, never a characteristic-two tensor of quadratic factors.

nodes.title: Domination of all lower-slot values
nodes.statement: In the preceding setup, w̃(a_d)>0 and w̃(a_d)>N w̃(a_i) for every i<d. These inequalities also hold after restriction to L, and q_a is still anisotropic over that restricted henselization.
hypotheses: N>0; all lower slots have nonnegative value.
proofSteps: If w̃(a_d)<2w̃(θ_N), the root α_N has negative value and a_d=(α_N θ_N)²(1−1/α_N); the principal-unit tail would be isotropic. Thus w̃(a_d)≥2N∑_{1≤i<d}w̃(a_i).

Not all slot values can vanish, by the dimension-unit-isotropy criterion and the real-place condition. The weak inequality therefore implies positive w̃(a_d) and the strict N-fold bounds, including i=0.
Restrict w̃ to L before entering Val(L). Comparison inequalities persist and the smaller henselization embeds in the larger one, so anisotropy descends.

sources.match: The domination statement uses restricted valuations on L; the auxiliary fields vary with N.

acceptance: A compactness argument on one space cannot use valuations on different L(α_N) without restriction.

nodes.title: A compact limiting detector
nodes.statement: Under the full hypotheses of Proposition 3.10 there is a valuation w_a on L, possibly of higher rank, such that q_a is anisotropic over L_{w_a}, w_a(a_i)≥0 for i<d, and w_a(a_d)>N w_a(a_i) for every N>0 and every i<d.
hypotheses: The form is anisotropic over L(α_N) for every positive N.
proofSteps: For each N take the subset of Val(L) cut out by those coefficient inequalities and henselian anisotropy. It is nonempty by nice-detection and the two preceding lemmas.
The comparison conditions are patch clopen, while henselian isotropy is patch open by Q2.7/henselian-isotropy-open; hence the anisotropy locus is closed.
Use compactSpace_patchTopology on Spv(L), with the LD.1 field-valuation dictionary, and the nested closed finite-intersection property. Do not impose rank one on the compact ambient space.

sources.match: Only the closed anisotropy locus and coefficient comparisons enter the compactness argument.

acceptance: The limit is not asserted to be a discrete valuation.

nodes.title: Coarsening to a constant-trivial divisor
nodes.statement: Let w_a be the compact detector above. Localize its valuation ring at p={x∈O_{w_a}:w_a(a_d)≤N w_a(x) for some N>0}, including x=0 by the infinite-value convention. The resulting coarsening w_L has a_d in its maximal ideal, every a_i for i<d a unit, and q_a anisotropic over L_{w_L}. Moreover w_L is trivial on k₁(t), hence on its relative algebraic closure in L, and is a prime divisor of the one-variable extension.
hypotheses: Use the domination bounds for all positive integers, not a finite bound.
proofSteps: Apply the LD.1 convex-subgroup/localization description of coarsening; p is prime, contains a_d and avoids every lower slot. The coarser henselization embeds in the finer one.
A nontrivial restriction to k₁ would be a non-dyadic global henselian valuation with a unit two-fold tail, contradicting Q2.6/dimension-unit-isotropy.

If restriction to k₁(t) were nontrivial, its relative algebraic closure F in L_{w_L} would be henselian of δ=d−1, with all d slots (a_{d−1},…,a₀) units and the real-place condition. The same imported criterion makes that subform isotropic, a contradiction.
A nontrivial valuation on a one-variable function field trivial on its constants is a curve place by AlgebraicCurves Layer 0 and the valuation dictionary.

sources.match: The dimension theorem must apply to the potentially non-finitely-generated henselian field F.

acceptance: A unit-isotropy theorem restricted to finitely generated fields does not suffice here.

nodes.title: Refined geometric prime-divisor detection
nodes.statement: Let H_d(K), L/K finite separable, k₁⊂K global, and u₂,…,u_{d−1} independent over k₁. Set t_i=u_i²−u_i. If a k₁,t-test form q_a for a_d remains anisotropic over L(α_N) for every N>0, with α_N²−α_N=a_d/(a_{d−1}⋯a₁)^{2N}, then there exists a prime divisor w_L of L trivial on k₁(t), such that w_L(a_d) is positive and odd and q_a remains anisotropic over L_{w_L}.
hypotheses: All slots are nonzero and the test ε-unit condition is retained.
proofSteps: Construct the compact limiting detector and coarsen it by coarsening-constant-trivial.
Because the other outer slots are now units, nice-parity forces the positive value of a_d to be odd.
Triviality on k₁(t) implies equal characteristic, so the divisor is geometric.

sources.match: The result is the precise strengthened detector consumed by the union-of-balls argument.

acceptance: The quantifier over every N>0 cannot be replaced by one sufficiently large N without an additional proof.

hypotheses: H_d(K); k₁ relatively closed global; t_i=u_i²−u_i for an independent tuple; a_d≠0.
proofSteps: Use auxiliary-root-fields and scalar extension of the imported quadratic form.
Translate the finite-degree extension tests using LD.0’s bounded-coordinate interpretation.

hypotheses: The same hypotheses and test presentation as anisotropy-set.
proofSteps: The positive divisor of nonzero a_d on the normal proper k_t-curve has finite support.
All lower slots belong to k_t× and hence have value zero. Apply nice-parity to obtain odd value on a_d.

nodes.title: The union-of-balls identity
nodes.statement: For the data defining b_a and V_a, b_a is exactly the union of B_w(a_d) over w∈V_a. The union of an empty family is empty.
hypotheses: H_d(K) and all Notation 4.1 admissibility conditions.
proofSteps: For τ∈b_a set L=K_τ. Apply refined-detection to this finite separable L/K, using all θ_N∈k_t×. Obtain w_L with positive odd w_L(a_d).

If 2w_L(τ)≤w_L(a_d), oddness makes it strict. The root β has negative value, so a_d=(a_dβ/τ)²(1−1/β) gives a principal-unit outer slot, contradicting anisotropy. Thus restriction w to K lies in V_a and τ∈B_w(a_d). This contradiction branch automatically has τ≠0.

Conversely, for τ in such a ball and θ∈k_t×, both root equations have positive-value right sides at w. Hensel lifting places both root fields inside K_w. Since q_a is anisotropic there it is anisotropic on K_{θ,τ}.

sources.match: The identity is a union, not an intersection, of strict valuation balls.

acceptance: If V_a=∅, then b_a=∅.
θ must range over k_t×, on which each detecting valuation is trivial.

nodes.title: The intersection-of-rings identity
nodes.statement: For the same data, O_a=Stab(b_a)=the intersection of O_w over w∈V_a. This is a subring, and is all of K when V_a is empty.
hypotheses: Finiteness of V_a and weak approximation for its pairwise distinct one-variable places are essential.
proofSteps: Each O_w preserves its own ball, so an element in all O_w preserves their union.

If x has negative value at one w, choose y at that ball’s minimum threshold, and prescribe at every other w′ a sufficiently low value so that xy lies outside B_{w′}(a_d). The pinned nonzero finite-order approximation theorem gives such y.
Then y belongs to the union but xy belongs to none of its balls. This excludes x from the stabilizer. No general rule about stabilizers of arbitrary unions is asserted.

sources.match: Weak approximation is the substantive bridge from the union identity to the ring intersection.

acceptance: For two independent places the union of their balls need not be additively closed, but its multiplicative stabilizer is the intersection ring.
The empty-family stabilizer equals K.

nodes.title: Isolation of each geometric divisor
nodes.statement: Every geometric prime divisor w of H_d(K) is V_a={w} for some admissible Notation 4.1 data. Consequently O_w=Stab(b_a).
hypotheses: The chosen k₁ and residue parameters depend on w; the resulting formula’s arity does not.
proofSteps: Use separating-parameters; replacing u by u²−u keeps the residue extension finite separable and gives k_t=k_u.

View K as a one-variable function field over k_t with relatively closed constants. Choose an odd m≥2 genus and use the pinned sole-pole theorem to get f whose only pole is order m at w. Set a_d=1/f; its only zero is w.
Apply test-abundance to choose ε and a tail anisotropic at w. The only possible member of V_a is w, and w is a member.
Apply stabilizer-intersection to the singleton.

sources.match: The chosen pole order must be both sufficiently large and odd; arbitrary approximation alone does not isolate the support.

acceptance: The sole pole is a sole zero after taking the reciprocal.
No smoothness claim over imperfect constants replaces the normal proper curve contract.

nodes.title: First-order niceness and unit triggers
nodes.statement: For each fixed d≥3, niceness of the global tail and the condition that every ε_i is a unit at each finite place with v(a₁)>0 are ring-formula conditions on the chosen definable global subfield and coefficient tuple. The formulas express the real-place and finite-place clauses of nice-form exactly.
hypotheses: The tail slots are nonzero and belong to the global subfield.
proofSteps: Quantify over the Rumely finite-valuation parameters. The dyadic condition is 2≠0 and 2∈m_v, so it is false in characteristic two. Translate v(a₀)≠0, v(a₁)<0 and unit conditions into membership and inverse membership, with explicit nonzero guards on inverted elements.

For henselian isotropy at a rank-one place, scale the coefficients to be integral and use a primitive integral vector x and a nonzero partial derivative D: either q(x)=0 already, or v(q(x))>2v(D(x)). Hensel applied in one coordinate gives a primitive zero. Conversely approximate a nonsingular henselian zero sufficiently closely by base-field coordinates, retaining primitivity and the strict inequality. Express strict comparisons by maximal-ideal membership of quotients. In characteristic two the nonsingular quadratic tail still has a nonzero partial derivative.

At real places the characteristic-zero tail is diagonal with entries 1,−a₀,−a₁,a₀a₁. It is anisotropic precisely at an ordering with both a₀ and a₁ negative. The absence of such an ordering is equivalent to −1 lying in the preordering generated by −a₀ and −a₁. Use the existing RealAlgebraicGeometry Layer 1 preordering-extension target, not a second proof plan here. A number field has Pythagoras number at most four by Hasse–Minkowski applied to five variables, so four squares for each of the four preordering coefficients gives a fixed finite formula.

This replaces the unjustified inference from henselian to base-field isotropy identified in inherited extraction E17; the local test is a Hensel witness, not an isotropic vector over the global field.

sources.match: The repair supplies the missing finite formula for the niceness clause used by Recipe 4.3.

acceptance: A tail isotropic over Q₂ but anisotropic over Q must pass the Q₂ test.
At a real ordering with both slots negative, the tail must fail niceness.
The same test works in characteristic two without diagonalizing a quadratic form.
In characteristic two, 2=0 belongs to every maximal ideal but no place is dyadic; the nonzero guard must prevent the dyadic trigger.

nodes.title: The guarded geometric-valuation formula
nodes.statement: At fixed d≥3 let raw_b(x) express x·b_a⊆b_a, with b_a defined using all nonzero θ in the definable relative constant field and the degree-at-most-four auxiliary root fields. Let G(b) assert all field, independence, slot, niceness and ε-unit conditions. Let V(b) assert that raw_b contains 0,1, is closed under addition, negation and multiplication, satisfies raw_b(x) or raw_b(x⁻¹) for each x≠0, and omits some element. Define val_d(x;b) to be G(b) and V(b) and raw_b(x).
hypotheses: All parameter blocks have length depending only on d; the interpreted global subfield has a fixed-length code.
proofSteps: Translate anisotropy into absence of a nonzero zero vector of the fixed-dimensional form, inside each interpreted auxiliary field. Use a finite disjunction for degrees one, two and four rather than assuming the root polynomials irreducible.

Degree-three symbols f∪α∪β in H³(K,μ_n^{⊗2}) are tested by whether β is a reduced norm of the prime-degree cyclic algebra (f,α)_n. The regular arithmetic surface Kato complex and the relevant local duality detect these symbols at horizontal divisors and finite arithmetic places, with an ordering-free formulation.

proofSteps: The prime-degree reduced-norm criterion is the specific Merkurjev–Suslin input needed in Pop §2A; it is not an application of mod-two Pfister symbols in characteristic two.

The classical Kato surface sequence at n=2 or 3, together with local duality and horizontal residues, is the input to Pop Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6. Record a supplier extension request at HL.6 and G-LOW until the exact sequence and norm criterion have been checked against their original proofs.

nodes.title: The low-dimensional shifted-ring construction
nodes.statement: For K=k(X) as above, choose f,α∈K× with α in the global base k and suitable δ∈k×. Put c_n=2n if char k≠2, and c_n=n=3 if char k=2. Let H_δ consist of β∈k× with v_s(β−1)>2v_s(c_n) at each finite base place where v_s(δ)≠0. Let H^f_{δα} be the subgroup of degree-three symbols f∪α∪β for β∈H_δ. For c∈k× and u∈K× put u_c=1+c(u−1) and u_{α,c}=u_c+αcⁿ(1−u)ⁿ. Define U^f_α by requiring that H^f_{δ*α} remain nonzero over K(ⁿ√u_c,ⁿ√u_{α,c}) for every c,δ*∈k×. On subsets of K use the shifted operations x*y=x+y−1 and x∘y=(x−1)(y−1)+1. Form X={u∈U:u*U⊆U}, then R={u∈X:u∘X⊆X}. These are fixed-arity definable predicates using the symbol-norm test.
hypotheses: The sets are formed after adjoining μ₂ₙ; root field factors and zero radicands are handled by finite degree cases. The auxiliary root fields have degrees 1,n,n², thus at most nine in characteristic two; use the general bounded-extension interpretation of LD.0, not only the degree-four adapter of FG.2.
proofSteps: Translate the nonzero-symbol condition by the reduced-norm obstruction from curve-symbol-inputs.

The integer c_n is nonzero in k and v_s(c_n)≥v_s(n). Hensel applied to Xⁿ−β at 1 therefore makes every β∈H_δ an n-th power at each excluded place. These local power conditions and strong approximation are the only uses of this bound in Pop Lemma3.6 and the subsequent shifted-ring proof. In characteristic two the threshold is zero; retaining the printed 2n would give an infinite threshold and even exclude β=1.
Use the globally definable H_δ predicates and quantify over every c and δ*.
Keep both stabilizations: the first is for shifted addition and the second for shifted multiplication. The shifted additive zero is 1 and shifted multiplicative unit is 2, even when 2=0 in K.

nodes.title: Key shifted-ring identity and singleton isolation
nodes.statement: For the good choices in Pop Key Lemma 4.7, R^f_α=1+⋂_{P∈D_{f,α}}m_P, where D_{f,α} consists of horizontal places with v_P(f) not divisible by n and α not an n-th power in the residue. Its multiplicative stabilizer is O_P.

proofSteps: Use Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6 to control U between local unit neighborhoods and symbol detection sets. Lemmas 4.3–4.6 identify the two shifted stabilizers and prove the displayed equality.

In dimension two the assertion holds in every characteristic without resolution.

nodes.statement: For a finitely generated field K with constant field κ and a transcendence basis T over κ, let A=O_κ in characteristic zero and A=κ otherwise. Let R_T be the integral closure of A[T] in K and S_T the integral closure of κ[T] in K. Equivalently R_T is the integral closure in K of the subring generated by T and the prime ring. Elements are tested by monic equations, not arbitrary polynomial equations.
hypotheses: T has length trdeg(K/κ), including length zero.
proofSteps: A is integral over the prime ring; transitivity of integrality proves the equivalent description of R_T.
Use the existing integral-closure carrier, with the embeddings of A[T] and κ[T] into K; do not identify the two base rings in characteristic zero.

nodes.title: Full geometric flags with an arithmetic terminal place
nodes.statement: In characteristic zero write e=trdeg(K/κ). A full geometric flag is a composition of e successive geometric prime divisors in the successive residue fields, with total ordered value group Z^e in lexicographic order and final residue κ_w finite over κ. Append any finite place v of κ_w and denote the composite by v∘w. Let V_T consist of all such composites for which every t∈T is in O_{v∘w}. If e=0 the geometric flag is the trivial valuation with residue K=κ, so V_∅ consists of the ordinary finite places of κ.
hypotheses: The family contains all flags and all terminal finite places satisfying T-integrality. Rank-one geometric divisors are not substituted for full flags.
proofSteps: Use the LD.1 residue-field interpretation and composition dictionary repeatedly exactly e times.
For a valuation ring O with maximal ideal m, O/m is represented by O modulo x−y∈m; compose with a residue valuation by taking its inverse image under the residue map.
Do not claim V_T is W_T: they have different ranks, and the source notation needs disambiguation here.

nodes.title: Full flags refine pole-detecting divisors
nodes.statement: In characteristic zero, every geometric rank-one divisor w of K containing T can be refined to a full geometric flag and then appended by a finite terminal arithmetic place so that the composite still contains T. In particular ⋂_{v∘w∈V_T}O_{v∘w}⊆S_T.
hypotheses: If e=0 the containment in S_T=K is automatic. The refinement assertion concerns e≥1.
proofSteps: For the residue field L of the first divisor choose a separating transcendence basis over the number field κ. Its size is e−1. Write the finitely many residues of T as fractions in the finite normalization of a localized polynomial base.

Shrink the base to remove its discriminant and the norms of these finitely many denominators. An étale point above a κ-rational base point then has finite separable residue κ′,and all the specified residues are regular there. Use FG.1/etale-specialization-input to embed the fraction field in κ′((π₂))⋯((π_e)).

The successive parameter valuations give the remaining e−1 geometric flag entries. Every specified residue stays integral. When e=1 this remaining flag is empty and the residue is already a number field.

All terminal residues of T are integral outside finitely many arithmetic primes of κ′. Choose a prime outside that set and append it. Any pole at the first divisor remains a pole in the composite lexicographic valuation. This proves the containment using geometric-intersection.

nodes.title: Arithmetic flags detect nonintegral coefficients
nodes.statement: For a number field κ, its integer ring A and an e-tuple T of independent variables, the intersection of all arithmetic composite rings in V_T inside κ(T) is A[T].
hypotheses: For e=0 this is the usual finite-prime intersection A=⋂_vO_v.
proofSteps: By flag-refinement an element f of the intersection lies in κ[T]. If f=0 there is nothing to prove. Otherwise at each finite prime v write f=cg with g∈O_v[T] having nonzero reduction and v(c) the least coefficient valuation.

Choose ζ∈(F̄_v×)^e with ḡ(ζ)≠0. A nonzero polynomial cannot vanish on the whole algebraic torus. The coordinates are roots of unity of order prime to the residue characteristic; lift them and pass to κ′=κ(ζ).

A regular-parameter flag at the closed point T↦ζ gives final geometric residue κ′. Append a prolongation v′ of v. Every t_i maps to a v′-unit and g maps to a unit, so the composite lies in V_T. If v(c)<0 it excludes f.
Thus all coefficient valuations are nonnegative. Treat e=0 directly rather than relying on a nonexistent positive-length flag.

For K/K₀ finite, every flag and terminal valuation prolongs and restriction gives a flag of the same geometric length; the T-integrality condition is preserved. Include all prolongations.

nodes.title: A uniform definable finitely generated normalization
nodes.statement: For each fixed Kronecker dimension d there is a fixed-arity ring formula defining R_T inside every finitely generated K of that dimension, for each transcendence basis T over its constants, with the characteristic-two resolution hypothesis only when d>3. R_T is a normal finitely generated ring and Frac(R_T)=K.
hypotheses: The formula may name T and the fixed-length codes used by its definable subfield families. It is uniform in those parameters, not a uniform choice of a transcendence basis.
proofSteps: In positive characteristic use R_T=S_T and geometric-intersection.

In characteristic zero use arithmetic-intersection and interpret each finite-length residue flag; apply the global finite-place formulas in the terminal number field. At e=0 use the integer-ring formula directly.

At fixed d the characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic lengths of T are d−1 and d. Use a finite characteristic split or pad tuples with dummy parameters with a stated guard. No formula quantifies over polynomials of unbounded degree.

acceptance: In Q(s), this gives Z[s]; the geometric intersection alone would incorrectly give Q[s].

nodes.title: Arithmetic coding in dimension-one normal domains
nodes.statement: Every infinite normal finitely generated domain of ring Krull dimension one is parametrically bi-interpretable with Z. In positive characteristic one may first use N and its usual bi-interpretation with Z.
hypotheses: Normality is retained in the sufficient version used here; ring dimension is not field Kronecker dimension.
proofSteps: In characteristic zero choose an integer basis of the integer ring of the fraction field. A nonzero integer clears denominators of each element; define its least positive suitable denominator and integer coordinate tuple, giving a definable injection into Z^{r+1}. The integer ring and Z are definable by the global arithmetic coding input.

In positive characteristic choose t by Noether normalization so the domain is finite free over F_p[t]. Define powers t^N, encode polynomial coefficients by prime-exponent arithmetic codes, and use the definable decoding map from Rumely p.211.

Use the arithmetic injection criterion in AKNS Proposition2.23/Corollary2.24. Arithmetic self-interpretations are definably homotopic to the identity (Lemma2.7),and the finite generating tuple makes two arithmetic presentations homotopic (Lemma2.26). Apply this to the injection just constructed. The original positive-characteristic decoding proof is the remaining G-RUM leaf.

acceptance: For an order enlarged by finitely many inverses, the least-denominator code is still finite and definable.

nodes.title: Finiteness of the relative arithmetic core
nodes.statement: Let B be a normal finitely generated domain with fraction field K. In characteristic zero put D=B∩κ. In positive characteristic choose t∈B transcendental over F_p and put D=B∩L, where L is the relative algebraic closure of F_p(t) in K. Then D is a definable, infinite, normal, finitely generated domain of ring Krull dimension one, hence Dedekind.
hypotheses: B is infinite; in positive characteristic this guarantees the existence of t. The global subfield L is relatively closed in K.
proofSteps: Use the fixed-size independence formulas to define D. Normality follows: an element of Frac(D) integral over D is integral over B, hence belongs to B and to the relative global subfield.

Use AKNS relative Noether normalization and generic freeness to place D inside a localization of a finite-type one-dimensional core. The one-dimensional intermediate-ring finiteness lemma then makes D finitely generated (AKNS Corollary 1.9 and Lemma 3.6).
Retain normality rather than inferring the Dedekind property solely from finite generation. The general nonnormal AKNS theorem is unnecessary for this roadmap’s normalizations.

nodes.title: Arithmetic bi-interpretation of normal finitely generated domains
nodes.statement: Every infinite normal finitely generated domain B is parametrically bi-interpretable with Z in the ring language.
hypotheses: The domain need not be a finite module over Z; its dimension can be arbitrarily large.
proofSteps: Use the definable arithmetic core D. Localize at c≠0 so B_c is finite over D_c[x₁,…,x_m] and free as a D_c-module. Choose finitely many generators y₁,…,y_n as a module over D_c[x₁,…,x_m], and a finite presentation over that polynomial algebra. Its free D_c-module may have infinite rank.

Every point a∈D_c^m lifts to a point (a,b) after a domain extension D′/D_c generated by at most n module elements. Two-generation of ideals in the Dedekind domain D_c makes this class of extensions uniformly interpretable by AKNS Lemma 2.11; Lemma 2.12 supplies the tensor-algebra codes.
Define the evaluation relation E(a,D′,b,e,p) by ideal membership p−e∈(x_i−a_i,y_j−b_j) in B_c⊗D_cD′. The union of such bounded-degree evaluations separates p,q∈B.

Use arithmetic rigidity of the interpreted D_c to match its copy in the double interpretation. Two elements correspond exactly when all their E-values correspond. This defines the comparison graph, giving both composites homotopic to the identity.

For the earlier coding inputs use the actual finite-tuple quotient construction:localization by the definable saturation of powers via Jacobson radicals (Lemma2.10),bounded relation matrices and multiplication constants (Lemma2.11),and flat base change of the relation module (Corollary2.12). Arithmetic finite-sequence codes are taken modulo equal decoding; a Gödel code need not be unique.

acceptance: Mutual interpretability alone is insufficient; the composite comparison graphs must be definable.

proofSteps: The graph from a field element x to its fraction class is xb=a; it is definable and total because Frac(R)=K.
The reverse graph sends r∈R to [(r,1)]. Translate the original R-predicate inside the interpreted fraction field, retaining its parameter codes.
Check both comparison graphs, rather than asserting that interpretation in both directions implies bi-interpretability.

nodes.statement: Every infinite finitely generated field of Kronecker dimension one or two is parametrically bi-interpretable with Z, in every characteristic and without any resolution premise.

proofSteps: Repeat normalization-definability using val₁ and val₂. In dimension one a number field uses its integer ring and a global function field uses the normalization of its polynomial ring.

In characteristic two and dimension two the divisor formula is the cubic-symbol curve formula, not a high-dimensional theorem used outside its stated range.
